Product liability law would point to the company that built the AI model, but AIs are trained on data the company didn't produce, and the legions of people who have used them also played a role. Free speech and social media immunity laws that treat an AI agent as responsible for its own actions could imply the AI agent deserves the same rights as a person.

Science.title: Even AI thinks it's a man's job: Models reveal gender bias in resumes and hiring assessments
Science.summary: The first hurdle may arise even before an application is submitted. A woman asks artificial intelligence to help her write her resume: The system chooses words, highlights qualities and builds a profile. Then another system, perhaps based on the same model, evaluates that text. If both reproduce gender stereotypes, the risk is a double filter: Bias enters the application and is reinforced by the person selecting it.

Science.title: Shrinking ruthenium catalysts boosts ammonia production rate up to 57-fold
Science.summary: Ammonia is drawing renewed attention as a "magic container" for safely storing and transporting hydrogen, a promising clean energy source of the future, as well as a carbon-free fuel that does not emit greenhouse gases when burned. However, for ammonia to be widely used as a key fuel, improving the efficiency of its production process is essential.

By utilizing the unusual properties of light particles, they can perform calculations that pose enormous challenges even for the most powerful supercomputers—or remain entirely beyond their reach. Science.title: Where in Europe could electric‑powered ferries create cleaner travel routes?
Science.summary: Electric battery-powered ferries use electricity from the shore to charge batteries on board. These batteries supply electric motors that propel the ship. On suitable routes, low-carbon electricity could make sea travel substantially cleaner and strengthen its potential as an alternative to flying.

Science.summary: It's that time of year when Christmas ads start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

Science.title: Reading the temperature fingerprints of electrocatalytic reactions
Science.summary: Electrocatalysis is key to turning renewable electricity into fuels and chemicals, and industrial electrolyzers typically operate at moderately elevated temperatures. Measuring how reaction rates change with temperature is also a powerful, yet underexplored, way to probe what controls them. Such measurements yield two quantities: an apparent activation enthalpy, reflecting the energetic cost of the reaction, and a prefactor, which is linked to the activation entropy.

Science.title: Today's Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country
Science.summary: It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England's first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God's providence.

Science.title: As Americans gather for Thanksgiving, a centuries‑old Sikh tradition offers an expansive vision of hospitality
Science.summary: On Sundays at Gurdwara Guru Nanaksar in Chapin, South Carolina, diners sit in rows on the floor while volunteers walk along each row carrying pots and trays of food. They pause to offer each person a spoonful of dal, a dish made with lentils, or a serving of vegetables. When the roti—a kind of flatbread—comes around, diners hold out both hands, palms up. A volunteer places the bread directly into their hands. This is "langar," the free communal meal served at Sikh houses of worship around the world.

Science.title: Protecting wild bees in Europe through calcareous grassland management and connected habitats
Science.summary: Calcareous grasslands are wildflower-rich ecosystems that develop on shallow, alkaline, nutrient-poor soils over chalk or limestone bedrock. They are rare and important habitats for wild bees and other pollinators—yet how well they can support these valuable communities depends on how they are managed. An international research team, led by the University of Göttingen, has shown that long-term abandonment or intensive management threatens the diversity of wild bees. Science.title: Webb confirms first-of-its-kind merger of a supergiant and smaller sun-like star
Science.summary: Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star on the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially "rejuvenated" star Bao. Their discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground.

Science.title: 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert
Science.summary: A remarkable 125,000-year-old discovery in Saudi Arabia reveals that early humans once thrived beside enormous lakes filled with wildlife in what is now a vast desert. Thousands of stone tools and ancient plant remains suggest these prehistoric people used sophisticated hunting techniques, potentially including weapons enhanced with poisonous plant compounds.

Science.title: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
Science.summary: MIT researchers have discovered that the brain’s natural waste-removal system becomes significantly less effective during sleep as people age. The decline is linked to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and changes in blood flow, potentially offering new clues about why aging increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Surprisingly, some older adults retain the same powerful cleansing waves seen in younger people.

Science.title: Young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing during first year at sea
Science.summary: New research has revealed young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing in their epic first year at sea, strengthening the case for proposed new marine protected areas. The study was co-led by France's CNRS, the Center Scientifique de Monaco and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. The international research team tracked 48 juvenile emperor penguins from three colonies around the Weddell Sea: Snow Hill Island, Jason Peninsula and Atka Bay.

Science.title: Wild barley's genetic diversity opens up new avenues for research and breeding
Science.summary: For the first time, an international research team coordinated by the IPK Leibniz Institute has characterized genomic diversity across the agriculturally important genus Hordeum. The study reveals how the genomes of barley and its wild relatives have evolved. These findings open up new avenues for systematically investigating this diversity and, in the long term, utilizing it for plant breeding. The results are published in the journal Nature.

Science.title: Midsize mussels fared the worst during the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome
Science.summary: During the record-breaking Pacific Northwest heat dome in 2021, a mussel's life depended on its size and location on the shoreline at Cattle Point on San Juan Island.

Science.title: Conservation of the tumour microenvironment across organs and species

Science.title: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s
Science.summary: Scientists have uncovered a powerful natural defense against Alzheimer’s disease that could open the door to new treatments. By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting its critical protective role.

Science.title: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors
Science.summary: A major breakthrough in superconductivity research has revealed that one of the essential ingredients for electricity to flow without resistance can exist at room temperature. Scientists discovered that electrons can form stable pairs at much higher temperatures than previously understood, suggesting that a different obstacle may be preventing room-temperature superconductivity.

Science.title: Gen Z men more likely than boomers to hold traditional views
Science.summary: A report published today from the King's Global Institute for Women's Leadership has found that young men in Britain are more likely to misperceive society's views on gender compared to other generations. Researchers found that Gen Z males are more likely to think society holds traditional views about them and therefore may be conforming to social expectations most Britons have left behind.

Science.title: Switching off cellular recycling gene increases yields of hard-to-make drug target proteins
Science.summary: With an unusual genetic modification that disabled cells' recycling systems, researchers found a way to make cells produce significantly larger amounts of the proteins used to discover and develop new medicines. The findings could help speed up drug development while reducing research and development costs.

Science.title: For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. Now we need to fill in what we left blank.
Science.summary: We need to understand how motherhood changes the brain, says neuroscientist Susana Carmona .

Science.title: Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb
Science.summary: When scientists shine a laser beam into a crystal, they typically expect a steady glow as the crystal's atoms are energized and begin to emit light. But in early 2024, while searching for something else entirely, researchers in the lab of Caltech's Andrei Faraon saw a crystal flash in a regular rhythm, like a metronome keeping a beat. The flashes came from billions of atoms embedded in the crystal. Coupled to a tiny superconducting circuit, the atoms had become synchronized and started emitting light together through a special quantum phenomenon known as superradiance.

Science.title: Electrified fabric captures phosphate for potential recovery from wastewater
Science.summary: When rain falls on farmland, lawns and gardens, it can wash phosphate from fertilizers into nearby waterways, triggering harmful algal blooms that cloud lakes and rivers, release toxins and rob the water of oxygen needed to sustain aquatic life. Now, Northwestern University and Argonne National Laboratory researchers have developed a reusable electrode that captures phosphate from water in laboratory tests, potentially recovering a valuable, nonrenewable resource while reducing water pollution.

Science.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
Science.summary: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.

Science.summary: The usual advice for people visiting wilderness areas is to leave nothing but footprints. But as our new study shows, even footprints may disturb rare ecosystems in Antarctica and cause irreversible changes.

Science.title: Bogong moths navigate with a light-dependent geomagnetic inclination compass
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11322-9 During their biannual migration, nocturnal Bogong moths (Agrotis infusa) rely on both a stellar and a geomagnetic compass for navigation, enabling them to maintain their migratory direction even if one of these cues is missing.

Science.title: Smart lighting technology enables remote color control
Science.summary: Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in Daejeon, South Korea, in November.

Science.title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
Science.summary: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support.
